title: Step-Size Stability in Stochastic Optimization: A Theoretical Perspective
claim: Plain gradient steps blow up as step size grows, while adaptive methods stay stable, and a stability index tracks this difference.
layout: 2 side-by-side line plots sharing x-axis, dashed vertical line marking best SGD step
description: Two line plots sit side by side on light gray grids, both with step size alpha on the x-axis. The left plot shows next-iterate loss f(x_{t+1}, s_t). The SGD curve (light blue) falls to a sharp minimum near alpha≈5, marked by a vertical dashed line, then climbs steeply past the dashed horizontal line for the starting loss. SPS (dark blue) drops and then stays flat at about 0.6. NGN (red) and SPP (green) decay smoothly toward zero. The right plot shows the stability index delta_t, with a legend for SGD, SPS, NGN and SPP. SGD grows linearly. The other three level off at about 2 to 3. The eye goes first to the SGD curve rising steeply in both panels, in contrast to the flat curves.
caption: Illustration of theory for f(x, st) = ln(1 + exp(−x)) + max{x−2, 0} and xt = −3. (Left) Next-iterate loss as a function of step size α. (Right) Stability index δt as a function of α. Vertical line marks best SGD step size. For large α, stable loss values coincide with benign (≈sub-linear) increase of δt.
abstract: We present a theoretical analysis of stochastic optimization methods in terms of their sensitivity with respect to the step size. We identify a key quantity that, for each method, describes how the performance degrades as the step size becomes too large. For convex problems, we show that this quantity directly impacts the suboptimality bound of the method. Most importantly, our analysis provides direct theoretical evidence that adaptive step-size methods, such as SPS or NGN, are more robust than SGD. This allows us to quantify the advantage of these adaptive methods beyond empirical evaluation. Finally, we show through experiments that our theoretical bound qualitatively mirrors the actual performance as a function of the step size, even for non-convex problems.
